getting_started.title: Getting started
getting_started.content:
Slate

Slate is the studio's pipeline and its people system in one window. Your studio may start it as the full suite, or as the VFX app or the Operations app, which show fewer screens. The help lists the screens of the app you opened.

GroupScreens
Production (VFX app) Build & Ingest, CAP Rename, Stock Viewer, Timeline Viewer, VFX Dashboard, Scheduling, Bidding
People and IT (Operations app) Attendance, Leave, Joining & Leaving, Hardware, Licences, IT Support, Deployment, Users & Roles, Admin Panel
In both Home, Settings, Tester Panel and Workspace Info (where your role has them)

What you see depends on who you are

There is no mode switch and no permission warning. A screen your role does not use is absent rather than greyed out, and some entries open a different screen for different people:

EntryMost people getHR or IT get
LeaveTheir balance and a request buttonThe approval queue as well, plus the calendar and the year end
IT SupportTheir own tickets and repliesThe service desk
Joining & LeavingNo entry at allTheir team's half of the checklist

So if somebody describes a button you cannot find, you are probably both right. A change to your role shows the next time you sign in.

Keyboard

KeysDoes
Ctrl+K or Ctrl+PSearch or jump: screens, actions and shots
Ctrl+1 … Ctrl+9Go to a sidebar entry by its position
F5 or Ctrl+RRefresh the screen you are on
Ctrl+Shift+SSettings
Ctrl+Shift+DDiagnostics: which database and shared folder this machine reached
F1Help for the screen you are on
F11Full screen
EscClose a dialog or this window

The sidebar folds to icons with the arrow at its foot, and a category heading folds its group away when you click it. Tables sort when you click a column heading, and most have a search box above them.

The header

The bell beside Help collects your notifications — shots assigned to you, new scans, replies to your requests. The number on it is what you have not read yet.

The dot and figure show the round trip to the studio database in milliseconds — single digits is a healthy network, three digits means something is congested.

Sync appears only when Slate is working offline on this machine's local copy (LOCAL MODE). It sends the changes you made offline to the studio database and brings everybody else's back. With the studio database connected every change is shared the moment it is saved, so there is nothing to sync and the button is not shown.

Leaving and signing out

If a screen has unsaved changes, or an ingest or rename is still running, Slate asks before it closes or signs you out. Signing out or closing Slate does not punch you out of Attendance.

When something is wrong

"Can't reach the studio database". A screen could not read from the database. Your work is safe; the screen fills in when the connection is back, and Try again asks straight away.

"LOCAL MODE". Slate could not reach the studio database when it started and is working on a local copy. You can keep working and nothing is lost, but nobody else sees it until you Sync. Tell IT.

"Could not open …" or "Could not load …". Something went wrong on that screen. Press Try again; if it keeps happening, press Copy details for IT and paste them into a ticket.

Anything else. Raise it in IT Support rather than messaging somebody — a ticket carries a clock; a message does not. Include the version from Workspace Info, the first thing IT will ask.

home.title: Home
home.content:
Home

The opening screen. It gathers what you are most likely to want first, from the screens you have — nothing on it opens anything your role cannot reach.

Quick launch

Tiles for your most-used screens. Only screens that are in your sidebar appear.

My recent tasks

Shots assigned to you on the dashboard, in any department. Click one to open it on the VFX Dashboard. "No shots assigned to you" means exactly that — it is not an error. If you believe you have work, the dashboard's Scope: My Shots shows the same list; assignment is by person, so ask the coordinator to check the shot is assigned to your account.

Live studio figures

Read from the studio database, so they are the same figures your supervisor sees:

FigureCounts
Active projectsProjects not marked finished or archived
Pending reviewShots sitting in a review status
People in todayPeople who have punched in today and not out
Open IT ticketsTickets not yet resolved, studio-wide
Upcoming leaveApproved leave starting in the next two weeks

In the Operations app Home also carries your punch in and out.

Every figure reading zero when you expect otherwise usually means LOCAL MODE rather than a quiet studio — a local copy has no studio in it. The header says when Slate is working offline.

workspace_info.title: Workspace Info
workspace_info.content:
Workspace Info

What this particular copy of Slate is running: the version, where it is installed, which database it actually reached, and which plugins loaded.

Why you would open it

To answer "which version are you on?" — the first question IT ask on any ticket, and the one nobody can ever answer. It is on this screen. Copying it into the ticket saves a round trip and often the whole investigation, because half of all reported faults are a machine that never took an update.

To check the plugin system. This tab is itself a plugin, shipped as a working example. If it is in your sidebar, the plugin machinery is healthy.

Reading it

The card lists the runtime context Slate handed the plugin: the signed-in user, the workspace root, and the active database mode.

Database mode is the line worth a glance. If it says SQLite and your studio runs PostgreSQL, this machine is on its local fallback copy. Everything will appear to work and none of it is reaching anybody else. That is worth a ticket on its own.

folder_creator.title: Build & Ingest
folder_creator.content:
Build & Ingest

Turn a client drive into a project, and keep feeding it as more arrives.

Building a new project

  1. Project Code / Name — PRJ_001, or whatever the studio uses. This becomes the top folder.
  2. Source — the client or incoming drive.
  3. Reel — leave it empty and Slate works it out from the folder names on the drive, or type one (REEL_01) to force it.
  4. Template — decides the folder structure every shot gets. Templates are chosen and managed on this screen.
  5. Press the build button.

Copy or move

Copy is the default: files are copied into the project and checked, and the client drive is left exactly as it was, so a failed ingest costs time and not data. Move is an option for when the source is a scratch copy you no longer need; the check before it starts says which one will happen.

The second delivery, and the third

Use Update & Ingest New Files from then on. Each delivery is brought in as a new scan version next to what is already there, so earlier plates are never overwritten and you can always see which delivery a frame came from.

While it is running

Pause, Resume and Stop act between frames, so a paused or stopped ingest never leaves a half-written plate.

You can leave the tab and do something else; the job carries on and the progress is there when you come back. If you close Slate or sign out while it is running, Slate asks first and, if you go ahead, stops it at the next safe point.

Image sequences

A 1,200-frame EXR sequence is one item to Slate, not 1,200 files. That is why the counts are smaller than the file count on the drive. A single still image is a still, not a sequence.

If something does not land

Files Slate cannot classify are listed in the report at the end of the ingest rather than dropped — unrecognised and ignored files are named there so you can place them by hand.

rename_tool.title: CAP Rename
rename_tool.content:
CAP Rename

Batch renaming, in two modes. Both build a full preview first, and the preview is the point: read it before you press the button.

Search and replace

Find a string anywhere in the filenames and replace it.

  • Find — shot_v01
  • Replace with — shot_v02
  • Case sensitive — when ticked, Shot will not match shot

The preview shows the old name and the new name side by side for every file it will touch. It is a preview, not an editor: to change a name, change the settings above it. If two files would end up with the same name, or a name is not allowed (slashes, ..), Slate says so and refuses the whole operation rather than overwriting one file with another.

Serialize (make sequence)

Renumber a set of files into a clean, padded sequence.

  • Base name — shot_010_v01_
  • Padding — the target number of digits. 4 gives 0001.
  • Start — the first frame number.

Useful when a vendor delivers frames numbered from something arbitrary, or with inconsistent padding that breaks every tool downstream.

One row per file

Every file is its own row in the preview, so you see exactly what each frame will be called.

Undo

Undo last rename puts the files of the last rename back under their old names. Renaming happens on disk, so still read the preview; if you are unsure, try it on a copy of a handful of files first.

If you close Slate while a rename is running, Slate waits for it to finish rather than leave files half renamed.

stock_browser.title: Stock Viewer
stock_browser.content:
Stock Viewer

The studio's stock library: footage, elements, textures — anything reused across jobs. Three panels: filters on the left, the gallery in the middle, the inspector on the right.

Finding something

Search reaches into the metadata as well as the filename, so 4K or smoke finds clips nobody thought to name that way.

Asset Filters in the sidebar narrow by type. Favorites keeps the handful you come back to. The library is paged, so a very large one loads as you scroll rather than making you wait for all of it.

The inspector

Select a clip and the right panel shows a preview and the facts you actually need before using it:

  • Resolution
  • FPS
  • Duration
  • Tags

These are read from the file itself, not typed in, so they are right even when the filename lies. Analyzing... means Slate is still reading it; the figures appear when it finishes.

Tags

Tags are how a library stays usable once it is large. They are shared with the studio rather than local to you, so tagging something well saves everybody else the search. Add them as you go — nobody ever comes back and tags a library later.

Adding to the library

Ingest brings a folder in. Fast Mode skips deep metadata analysis and is much quicker on a big drop — the clips are usable immediately and the detail fills in later. Pause works mid-ingest.

Refresh Library re-reads what is on disk, for when somebody has added files outside Slate.

Import and Export move a library definition between machines. Clear Library empties it entirely — it asks first, and it means the whole library, not the current filter.

Thumbnails

Generated in the background the first time an item is seen, then cached. A fresh library is slow to look at once and quick every time after.

A thumbnail that never appears usually means a format FFmpeg on this machine cannot read. Everything else about the item still works, and it is worth a ticket so IT can check the FFmpeg build.

shot_review.title: Timeline Viewer
shot_review.content:
Timeline Viewer

The reel laid out in order: plates reel by reel, with each department's render on its own layer directly beneath the plate it came from.

The shots come from the dashboard, so the timeline is always built from what production is actually tracking — not from whatever happens to be sitting in a folder.

Building a lineup

Pick the project and the reel. Slate finds the current version of each shot and lays them out in shot order.

Playing it

Heavy EXR and DPX sequences are transcoded to a proxy in the background the first time, then scrub smoothly. The first play of a new shot waits for that once; every later play does not.

Cutting

Launch Editor opens the lineup in Olive, embedded inside the Slate window. If Olive is not installed the button is absent and Slate falls back to its own player — ask IT to run setup.bat, which fetches it.

Reviewing

Review happens in OpenRV, which is what the studio actually reviews in. The dashboard opens a shot there directly with its Review in RV button, and a verdict recorded in RV comes back into Slate against that shot.

There used to be a Shot Checker built into this tab. It is gone, on purpose — a second-rate viewer beside a real one only splits where notes end up.

dashboard.title: VFX Dashboard
dashboard.content:
VFX Dashboard

Every shot in the project, its status, and who has it. This is the screen production actually runs the job from.

Reading it

The chips along the top count the reel by status: Approved, WIP, Review, YTS, Retake, Omit, Final, Done. They respond to whatever filter is on, so they always describe what you are looking at rather than the whole project.

Each department gets its own column — DMP, CG, Roto, Prep, MMV and the rest. A cell holds that department's status on that shot, so you can read one shot across or one department down.

Narrowing it

ControlDoes
ScopeAll, My Shots, or My Dept — your own department, worked out from your role
StatusOne status across the reel
GroupCollapse by reel, artist or department
AdvancedCombine them — everything in Matchmove that is WIP and assigned to nobody
Board ViewThe same data as columns by status instead of a table

"No matching shots" means the filter excluded everything, not that the project is empty. Clear the filters before concluding anything.

Changing something

Edits are held locally until you press Save Changes, so a mis-click is not instantly everybody's problem. The header counts unsaved change(s) and warns that these edits are not in the database yet. The button only lights up when there is something to save.

Leaving the tab with unsaved changes keeps them. Closing Slate or signing out with unsaved changes asks first, and offers to save them.

Where the data lives

The studio database, or an Excel sheet where a show still runs that way. The header says which.

In database mode other people's changes arrive without a refresh. In Excel mode the sheet is the truth, and Excel backup in the header shows when a copy was last written. FAILING there means the sheet is locked, missing, or on a share this machine cannot reach — worth fixing straight away, because that backup is the only thing standing between a crash and a day of retyping.

LOCAL MODE: no synced shots yet means this machine is on its local fallback database. Nothing you change here is reaching anybody.

scheduling.title: Scheduling
scheduling.content:
Scheduling

Who is on what, and when.

Assignments here are the same records the dashboard shows against each shot. There is one record, not two — assigning somebody in one place shows up in the other immediately.

Approved leave is on the plan

Somebody with approved leave shows as away for those dates. This is the whole reason the pipeline and the people system are one application: a plan that does not know about leave is a plan that breaks the week somebody goes on holiday, and nobody finds out until the Monday.

Pending leave is not shown as away, because it has not been decided yet. If you need it decided, chase the approver rather than planning around a request that may be refused.

What to watch

Somebody scheduled across a date they are already away is the thing to look for. The plan will let you do it — sometimes you genuinely need to, and somebody will move their leave — but it should be a decision rather than a surprise.

bidding.title: Bidding
bidding.content:
Bidding

What a job should cost, before it is agreed.

Building one

Build the bid out of shots and the work each one needs by department. Slate totals days and cost as you go, so the effect of adding ten more roto shots is visible while you are deciding rather than afterwards.

When it becomes a job

A bid that turns into a job carries its shot list into the project, so the dashboard starts with the shots that were actually quoted rather than a blank sheet somebody retypes from a PDF. Retyping is where shots go missing.

Keep it after delivery

The gap between what was bid and what the dashboard ended up recording is the only honest input to the next bid. A studio that deletes its bids estimates the next job from memory, and memory is consistently optimistic.

attendance.title: Attendance
attendance.content:
Attendance

Punch in when you start and out when you finish. That is the whole screen.

It is not only a record

If your studio operates comp-off, this is what earns it. Slate reads the punch data and credits the ledger from it — never typed in by hand, and never credited twice for the same day.

Three ways a day qualifies, and a studio may operate any combination:

  • You worked a weekly off (Sunday)
  • You worked a public holiday, as listed in HR's calendar
  • You worked a long enough shift

A shift that crosses midnight is counted properly rather than discarded as bad data. In a crunch week that is usually the shift that earned the comp-off in the first place, so throwing it away would defeat the point.

If you forgot to punch

You cannot edit your own record, deliberately. Ask HR — a record anyone can correct is not a record, and comp-off is calculated from it.

Where it surfaces

Your comp-off balance is the fourth figure on the Leave screen. If your studio does not operate comp-off it reads zero and says so underneath, which is correct rather than broken.

leave.title: Leave
leave.content:
Leave

Two entirely different screens sit behind this entry. Which you get depends on whether you approve other people's leave.

Asking for leave

The four figures

FigureMeans
AvailableWhat you can actually take right now
AccruedEarned since you joined — two days for every completed month
Awaiting approvalDays held by requests nobody has decided yet
Comp offEarned from attendance, where the studio operates it

Available already has your pending requests subtracted. Ask for five days and then five more before the first is decided, and the second is measured against what would be left. That is on purpose — it stops people accidentally spending the same days twice.

Accrual counts completed months from your actual joining date. Join on the 15th and your first two days arrive on the 15th of the next month, not at the end of this one.

Why a day off sometimes costs three

Press Request leave and the dialog shows the cost before you commit to it.

The studio works Monday to Saturday; Sunday is the weekly off. Public holidays are free. But a working day sitting between two non-working days, that you do not come in for, charges the whole block — the sandwich rule:

Mon  holiday
Tue  working day   <- you take this off
Wed  holiday

charged: 3 days, not 1

It reaches further than you would expect. If that Monday holiday follows a Sunday, the Sunday is in the block too, and the same day off costs four.

The dialog spells this out as you pick the dates, and writes the reason underneath the number. If the figure surprises you, the explanation is already on screen. A half day costs 0.5.

What happens next

Your request goes to your supervisor first, then to HR. It is only deducted once both have said yes.

The Waiting on column says whose desk it is on. A rejection always carries a reason — Slate will not let anyone reject a request without writing one.

What a request cost is frozen when you submit it. If the studio changes a holiday afterwards, it cannot retroactively change what you were deducted.

Approving leave

The screen opens on Waiting on me. Sorting is deliberate: yours first, then soonest starting, because somebody leaving on Monday needs an answer before somebody leaving next month.

Four figures: waiting on you, elsewhere in the chain, away today, and the all-time total.

You can only act on requests at your own stage. Selecting one still with the other approver leaves the buttons switched off rather than failing when you press them.

Approve tells you where it goes next before you confirm, because approval means different things at the two stages — a supervisor is passing it on, HR are spending the days. Reject asks for a reason, and the person who asked will read exactly what you write.

HR only: Calendar

The studio's public holidays. Every date on this list is free for everybody, and the sandwich rule is measured against it, so it changes what leave costs across the whole studio. Worth doing in one sitting at the start of the year.

Add a date, a name, and who it applies to — All, or a single location for a site-specific holiday. Past holidays are dimmed so your eye stays on the rest of the year.

Removing a holiday does not rewrite history: leave already taken keeps the day count it was charged at. Only future requests change.

HR only: Year end

The one destructive action in the module, so it previews first and confirms second.

Closing a year draws a line under it. Up to the carry-forward cap (12 days by default) moves into the next year; anything above it is lost. The table shows, per person, the balance at year end, what carries and what lapses — with the lapsing column in red — before anything is written.

  • It defaults to the year just gone. Closing the year you are still in lapses leave people have not had a chance to take.
  • A year already closed is never closed twice; those people show as already closed and are skipped.
  • After a close, balances count from the line: accrual restarts, the carried days are the opening balance, and leave taken before the line is not deducted again.

Without a year end, the carry-forward cap never actually applies. It is a policy you believe you have rather than one the software enforces.

joining_leaving.title: Joining & Leaving
joining_leaving.content:
Joining & Leaving

One checklist, read in two directions. HR and IT each see their own half and neither is shown work they cannot do.

Starting somebody

HR only. Start joining puts a person on the list: pick them, say whether they are staff or freelance, and name the department.

Freelancers skip payroll and final settlement automatically. The rest of the list is identical.

IT do not start people, and that division is the point — IT provisioning somebody nobody hired is exactly how ghost accounts happen.

The two halves

HR's linesIT's lines
Signed contract received
ID and address proof on file
Added to payroll (staff only)
Studio induction and policies
Introduced to the team		 Domain account created
Email and calendar set up
Workstation issued
DCC software installed
Project shares mounted
Render farm access

The Yours column counts what is outstanding on your list; All counts both teams. All is the one that tells you whether somebody is actually ready to start.

People are sorted with the most outstanding work first, so the person who needs attention is at the top rather than in alphabetical order.

Issuing a machine

IT only. Select the person, press Issue machine, pick from what is free. Slate then does four things at once:

  • writes the assignment, with the date and your name
  • marks the machine Active in Hardware against that person
  • ticks Workstation issued on the checklist
  • stamps the machine name on that row

The last one is why leaving works at all. When that person goes, the leaving checklist already knows which machine to ask for. Nobody has to remember, and nobody has to search an inventory for a name.

A machine flagged Repair is never offered, and collecting one back does not clear that flag — it is free of its owner but not free to hand to somebody else.

When somebody leaves

Start leaving lays down the mirror image. Not a different list — the same list undone:

Granted on the way inRevoked on the way out
Domain account createdDomain account disabled
Project shares mountedProject shares unmounted
Render farm accessRender farm access revoked
Workstation issuedWorkstation returned

Every access granted on the way in has a matching revocation on the way out. That pairing is the only reason offboarding can be systematic rather than approximate, and it is checked by the test suite so a task added to one side cannot quietly be left without its mirror.

Kit not returned

A red card appears at the top of the screen when a machine is still out with somebody who is being offboarded. It is only there when it is true.

For a studio that cycles freelancers per project this is where the money is. A machine nobody asked for back is invisible until something asks the question.

it_support.title: IT Support
it_support.content:
IT Support

Your own tickets, or the whole queue, depending on whether you work in IT.

Raising one

Two questions decide how fast it gets picked up. Answer them honestly rather than strategically — you do not choose the priority, and that is exactly what keeps the queue worth trusting.

Who is affected?

  • The whole studio, or a service everyone depends on
  • My department, or several people
  • Only me

Can you carry on?

  • I cannot work at all — there is no way around it
  • I have a workaround, but it is costing me real time
  • I can carry on. This can wait.

Slate derives the priority from those two answers:

Cannot workWorkaroundCan wait
Whole studioP1P2P2
A departmentP2P3P3
One personP3P3P4

Write what you were doing and what happened, and include the version from Workspace Info. "It crashed" cannot be acted on.

Afterwards

The ticket shows who picked it up, or Not yet picked up if nobody has. Open it to read the conversation and reply.

When IT need something from you it moves to Waiting on you. Watch for that one — the clock is paused on their side and running on yours, and a ticket can sit there for days because nobody noticed.

Working the queue

It opens sorted the way you should work it: breached first, then at risk, then by priority, then by how little time is left. Five figures across the top — Open, Breached, At risk, Unassigned, Mine.

PriorityRespond withinResolve within
P115 minutes4 hours
P230 minutes8 hours
P32 hours3 days
P44 hours5 days

Response is attention; resolution is a fix. They are separate on purpose — telling somebody you have seen it and it will be tomorrow is a good outcome, and the clock should recognise that.

Take assigns it to you. Mark responded stops the response clock — press it when you actually reply, not when you open the ticket. Unassigned is the figure to watch: a ticket nobody owns is a ticket nobody is working.

hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.content:
Hardware

Machines the studio owns, who has them, and their state.

Status

StatusMeans
AvailableIn stock, free to issue
ActiveIssued to somebody and in use
RepairWith a workshop. Cannot be issued, and collecting it back does not clear the flag

Finding a machine

Search by machine name, person, location, CPU or GPU, filter by status, and click a column heading to sort. The list refreshes by itself when somebody else changes it, and keeps your selection.

Issue and Collect

Select a machine and press Issue to… to hand it to somebody, or Collect to take it back. Both write the loan record that the leaving checklist reads, so when that person leaves, Slate already knows which machine to ask for. (Joining & Leaving can issue a machine too, and it writes the same record.)

Who has a machine is never typed into the machine's own details — a name typed there would not create the loan, and nothing would ever ask for it back.

Adding machines

+ Add PC adds one by hand. Sync from Live Ops imports machines running Slate that the inventory does not know yet, with their specification; they arrive unassigned. Double-click a machine to edit it.

What to check now and then

Machines marked Active against somebody who has left. Joining & Leaving shows these as Kit not returned.

licences.title: Licences
licences.content:
Licences

Not an inventory. This screen answers the two questions you actually get asked, and they cost money in opposite directions:

  • Are we licensed? More people working than seats bought is what ends in an audit letter.
  • Are we paying for seats nobody uses? Invisible until somebody looks at the peak rather than the total.

Peak, not total

The honest measure of a floating licence is peak concurrent use. Twenty artists and eight Nuke seats is perfectly fine if never more than eight are comping at the same moment — and the only way to know is to have written the number down repeatedly.

Record usage does that: pick the product, type what the licence server is reporting right now. Take the reading when the studio is busy. A quiet-afternoon number makes an over-subscribed licence look perfectly healthy, which is the one mistake that matters here.

The window selector at the top — 30 days, 90 days, a year — decides how far back the peak is measured.

The findings

FindingMeans
Over-subscribedPeak exceeded what we own. Outranks everything else, including an expiry — an expiry is a diary entry, a shortfall is people unable to work
ExpiredAlready gone. Anyone relying on it is stuck right now
Renews soonInside 45 days. Decide before purchasing needs lead time
Under-usedPeak never reaches 60% of what was bought. Seats to drop at renewal
No readingsBought, never measured. Nothing to renew against except the invoice

Rows are sorted worst first, so the audit risk sits above the housekeeping.

Every row says what it means

Not just a status word but a sentence in numbers — "Peak use reached 9 against 8 seats", "Never more than 5 of 10 in use at once; 5 seats are being paid for and not worked with".

That is deliberate. A status word on its own is not something you can take to purchasing, and the whole point of keeping readings is to hold the renewal conversation with evidence instead of instinct.

The figures at the top

Short of seats and Renewals to decide are the two to act on. Never used at once totals the spare seats across every product that has been measured — that number is what a renewal could be cut by.

deployment.title: Deployment
deployment.content:
Deployment

A record of what was installed where — Nuke 16 on WS-12, a plugin update on the comp floor. Slate does not install software itself; this is the log IT keep so the studio knows what each machine should have.

Recording one

  1. + Record deployment: the package and the machine. It starts as Pending.
  2. When you know how it went, select it and press Mark Success or Mark Failed.

The figures at the top count every record and the success rate of the ones that have finished; pending ones do not count as failures.

Finding one

Search by package, machine or person, filter by status, and sort by any column. Other people's records appear without a restart.

Updating Slate itself

New versions of Slate reach machines through the studio's update path, not through this screen. Check Workspace Info on a machine for the version it is actually running.

users_roles.title: Users & Roles
users_roles.content:
Users & Roles

Who exists, and what each of them can reach. HR see Users; the people who edit permissions see Roles & Permissions.

Roles decide screens

A role carries the tabs it opens and the things it may do. A tab somebody has no business on is absent, not greyed out. A change to somebody's roles shows the next time they sign in.

Who may give what

Admin and Developer may give anything. Anybody else can only hand on what they hold themselves: they cannot tick Full access or the sensitive abilities (managing users and permissions, system administration, studio settings, destructive test tools, deleting projects), cannot change a role they hold, and cannot give somebody a role more powerful than their own — or change the account of somebody more powerful. Boxes you cannot give are switched off, and the reason is in the tooltip.

Adding somebody

Create the person here, then start them in Joining & Leaving. The account on its own is not onboarding — the contract, the machine and the accesses all need tracking, and that is the screen that tracks them.

Passwords

Stored as one-way hashes. You can reset somebody's password; you cannot read it, and neither can anyone else, including an administrator.

Somebody who has left

Deactivate rather than delete. The account is switched off, their attendance, leave and other history are kept, and they disappear from lists and pickers. Show deactivated brings them back into view, and Reactivate switches the account on again. A person whose last working day has passed counts as deactivated too.

Deactivating is refused while the person still has leave waiting for a decision or a machine issued — handle those first. You cannot deactivate yourself. Delete is only for an account made by mistake that has no history at all.

admin_panel.title: Admin Panel
admin_panel.content:
Admin Panel

The studio's machinery: the workstations, their logs and the database. Supervisors see Live Ops read-only; the rest is for Admin and Developer.

Live Ops

Every workstation running Slate reports in: who is signed in, what it is doing, its specification and when it was last heard from. A machine that stops reporting drops out of the live view.

From here an administrator can send a message to every workstation, export a Fleet report, start the API gateway and clear the thumbnail and proxy caches on every workstation (Wipe caches, which asks first).

Audit Logs

What happened and who did it: the logs workstations send in (so a fault on somebody's machine can be read without visiting it), the change history of shots, and the audit trail of account and permission changes. This is the first place to look when a ticket says "it crashed" and nothing else.

Data Center

The studio database itself: its tables, their contents and the tools that act on them directly. Changes here bypass every screen's checks and affect everybody at once, so it is for Admin and Developer only, and it asks before anything destructive.

tester.title: Tester Panel
tester.content:
Tester Panel

Tools for checking Slate itself. Nothing here is needed to do a day's work. Most of them write files into a folder you choose — point them at a scratch folder, never at a project or a studio share. The destructive tools are for Developer accounts only.

Data Generator

Writes dummy files (plates, renders, other types) into a target folder, to test ingest and browsing on realistic data.

Workflow Sim

Builds a test incoming structure and a matching Excel sheet, with optional complications, to run an ingest against.

Structure (Chaos)

Creates deliberately awkward folder structures — deep nesting, odd names — to check that ingest copes.

Analysis

Compares a result folder with its source after a test run, and checks the database: an integrity check, and VACUUM to compact it.

Diagnostics

A live view of the system log, and stress tests such as generating many thumbnails at once.

System

The permission matrix as Slate currently sees it, temporary in-memory configuration overrides, and a tool that changes file dates in a target folder (to test anything that depends on age).

Automation

A one-click regression run: generate, ingest, verify.

Utilities

Clears the tester folder the other tools write into.

settings.title: Settings
settings.content:
Settings

Two kinds of setting live here. Your preferences apply to you on this machine. Studio settings apply to everybody and are shown only to the people allowed to change them (Admin, Developer and IT).

Your preferences

  • Restore sessions — reopen the folders you last used.
  • Dry run — rehearse file operations without writing anything.
  • Theme and UI scale — how Slate looks on this screen.
  • Open Nuke as — which Nuke opens when you open a shot in Nuke.

Press Save changes; what applies at once and what needs a restart is said when you save.

Studio settings

Studio Policy — what counts as late and how long a normal day is. Attendance and Leave both read these, for everybody.

Paths & Connections — the project and server roots, the studio logo in the header, and where the studio database is (host, port, name, user). The database details are stored in this machine's Slate configuration file, so an update keeps them. If Slate starts in LOCAL MODE, look here — though it is usually the server or the network rather than these values.

Updates — check whether a newer Slate is available.

Runtime status and maintenance

Runtime Status shows which database this machine reached, whether the shared folder is reachable and whether offline changes are waiting to sync. The maintenance tools make a project report, back up a project, and open the log folder for IT.

Your password

Change it from your name in the header. It is stored as a one-way hash: nobody, including an administrator, can read it back.
